title: Mercosur’s Tax Break Is Fueling Brazil’s Oil Push Into Europe | OilPrice.com
text:
EU Moves to Overhaul Emergency Oil Stockpiles

Natalia Katona is a freelance commodity analyst, based in the United Arab Emirates.

This year Brazil is set to add more oil than any other producer in the world. And this offshore production boom came at the right time for a global oil market that has been short of barrels reaching refiners without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Brazilian crude output hit a record 4.7 million b/d in September, up 20.3% year-on-year. Historically, a major part of Brazil’s first exports went to Asia.

It’s no surprise that the first price assessments for Brazilian grades came about in China, a country that dominated the early years of Brazilian exports. However, Brazil’s incremental supply is forcing the state-owned company Petrobras and other producers to diversify their pool of buyers, looking beyond Asia. After the ban on Russian crude imports in 2022, Brazil has started making inroads into Europe, with this year seeing unprecedented levels of crude flows to the Old Continent.

Brazil will need buyers both in Asia and Europe as more offshore capacity comes online. Since October 2024, state-controlled Petrobras has brought six major projects into production, including new units at the giant Buzios and Mero fields. Together with Equinor’s Bacalhau, those projects account for roughly 1.3 million b/d of capacity, some of which is still ramping up. Petrobras is expecting two more Búzios platforms, P-80 and P-82, to start producing in 2027. Hence, for Brazilian producers, the question is where they can sell those additional barrels at the best return after freight and taxes.

Until this year, freight accounted for much of the difference between selling to Europe and selling to Asia. That changed in March, when the Brazilian government introduced a 12% crude export tax after the US-Iran war sent oil prices into triple-digit territory. Calculated on the FOB value of the cargo, the new tax allowed the Brazilian administration to capture part of the windfall and, in turn, subsidize the prices of diesel as the Latin American giant remains dependent on imports from abroad. The government has since extended it three times, most recently through December 31.

Brazil’s export tax eventually turned out to be Europe’s advantage. The EU secured preferential terms under its interim trade agreement with Mercosur this year. Signed in January and provisionally applied from May 1, the agreement requires Brazil to reduce qualifying export duties by at least 50% for EU-bound shipments. At a FOB price of around $77/bbl, a Brazilian producer pays $4.62/bbl in tax on a sale to the EU against $9.24/bbl on a sale to China or India. That leaves room to offer a European refiner a price marginally below market levels and still earn more on the barrel.

By August, EU-bound loadings had reached 975,000 b/d, almost double pre-crisis February’s 490,000 b/d. The EU’s share of Brazilian exports rose from 22% to roughly 34% over the same period. Brazil ranked fifth among the EU’s crude suppliers, behind the US, Norway, Kazakhstan and Libya. Discounts on Tupi and Búzios have made both grades cheaper for European refiners than Norway’s Johan Sverdrup even after freight. Brazilian cargoes have gone to the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region, Spain, Portugal, Poland, France and Italy. Even Norway took in some Brazilian crude, although shipments there do not qualify for the EU tax rate.

Whilst historically Brazil’s crude exports were mostly revolving around Tupi and Buzios, the recent boost in second-generation giants such as Mero has provided European refiners with additional flexibility to choose their most convenient grade. Mero flows have almost tripled between 2024 and now to 570,000 b/d and the 29° API grade is increasingly becoming Europe’s favorite. Its sulphur content is the lowest amongst Brazil’s top three grades (0.31%), making it the most convenient option for coastal refiners seeking to produce IMO 2020-compliant VLSFO. Moreover, with Mero wielding the lowest metal content readings amongst Brazil’s main grades, any incremental volumes from the Mero platform could find a stable outlet in Europe.

Europe gained a further advantage when tanker rates surged in September and October. Brazil uses Suezmax-sized shuttle tankers to collect crude from offshore production units and deliver it to larger vessels or terminals such as Açu and Angra dos Reis. Most Asia-bound barrels make the onward voyage on VLCCs, while Suezmaxes carry more than half the cargoes heading to Europe. That distinction mattered in October. Longer voyages kept VLCCs occupied for more days, just as Gulf exporters needed more of them for short shuttle runs through Hormuz to transfer crude to other tankers in the Gulf of Oman.

Consequently, Brazil-to-China VLCC freight jumped from $6/bbl in February to $36/bbl in October. Meanwhile, Suezmax freight to Europe rose from around $6.50/bbl over the summer to $28/bbl at the freight rally’s October peak, still $8/bbl below the cost of shipping to China. However, considering Q3 purchases were made in the low-freight summer months, Europe-bound loadings fell to 400,000 b/d in September before recovering to 640,000 b/d in October. Total Brazilian crude exports dipped to 2.80 million b/d in September and rebounded to 2.95 million b/d the following month.

Shipment timing may explain some of the monthly swings, but the unsold November cargoes showed what high freight was costing producers. Brazilian (as well as West African) sellers had to offer deeper discounts at the loading port to keep their crude competitive on arrival. By mid-October, Tupi FOB Brazil was trading around $25/bbl below ICE Brent. The discount has since narrowed to around $15/bbl as tanker rates have eased; however, even after the rebound, differentials are still $10/bbl below summer rates.
